title: Vows
hook: monks and nuns vow poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability

segments.voice: Yesterday, confession rites: before an icon, to a priest in private, or a whole room kneeling. Your line was we have left undone.

A man in a plain black habit stands at the altar of a monastery church. In front of his brothers, he signs a sheet of paper he has written out by hand and lays it on the altar. Then he lifts his arms and sings a single line from the Psalms, asking God to uphold him so that he may live, and not be put to shame in his hope. The monks sing it back, and again. Then he lies down on the floor while they pray. When he gets up, he belongs to that community for good. Today: vows.

A vow is a promise made to God, out loud, meant to be kept, and some Christians make vows that shape their whole lives. Start with a story. In Matthew, a rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks, and Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." The young man goes away sorrowful. But according to his biographer Athanasius, a young Egyptian named Antony heard that same verse read in church, gave away his land, and began a life of prayer. Next, what they vow. In Catholic religious life the classic vows are poverty, chastity and obedience: owning nothing of your own, not marrying, and listening for God's will through the community and its leaders. Benedictines, following the Rule of Saint Benedict, vow stability, staying with one community; conversion of life; and obedience. Stability means no running away when the brothers get on your nerves. Orthodox monks and nuns make vows too, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran communities. Then, how seriously. Ecclesiastes warns: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Communities go slowly too, testing someone a long time before the final vow. Last, how publicly. A psalm says, "I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people." The paper on the altar says the same. Not a private resolution. A whole life, given wholly, with witnesses.

segments.voice: Make one vow small enough to keep, for today only: no phone at dinner, or one kind word to someone who irritates you. Say it once, quietly, out loud, so it's a promise and not just a thought. If you pray, make it to God; if you don't, make it to yourself, with this minute as your witness.
Vows. Promises made to God out loud before witnesses, like poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability: a life given over on purpose.
Your line: given wholly. Kept for a day, or kept for life. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Catholic monks, nuns, friars and sisters profess vows such as poverty, chastity and obedience, and Benedictines vow stability, conversion of life and obedience, after a long period of testing; Orthodox monastics and some Anglican and Lutheran communities also take vows.

chat.says: Why would a monk promise to stay in one monastery his whole life?
options: It's the Benedictine vow of stability: staying with one community, no running away when it's hard.
It's a punishment for past sins; the community keeps him there until he's paid them off.
It's only a habit of the past; no Christian community asks for vows like that today.
chat.meaning: Benedictines vow stability: staying with one community. It means no running away when the brothers get on your nerves.

notes: Hook follows the Rule of Saint Benedict ch. 58 (written petition laid on the altar; the 'Suscipe me' from Psalm 119:116 / Vulgate 118:116, sung and repeated by the community). The prostration while the community prays is current practice in some monasteries, not in the Rule; confirm or cut. The Rule has the verse sung three times; the script avoids the count.
Athanasius, Life of Antony 2 (paraphrased): Antony heard Matthew 19:21 read in church and gave away his inheritance. Confirm the paraphrase.

'In Catholic religious life the classic vows are poverty, chastity and obedience' (the evangelical counsels); Benedictine vows from RB 58 (stabilitas, conversatio morum, obedientia). Confirm the explanation of obedience and stability.
howItsDone says 'after a long period of testing'; confirm or soften to 'a long time'.
Original: נֶדֶר appears in Ecclesiastes 5:3 in Hebrew numbering (5:4 KJV); the note avoids a verse number. Confirm.

Audit pass: original note corrected: the warning verse (KJV 5:5) uses the verb (tiddor); the noun neder is in the verse before (KJV 5:4). The remaining causal 'So communities go slowly' (Ecclesiastes as the reason for novitiates) softened to 'Communities go slowly too'. Note: RB 58 does describe the novice prostrating at each monk's feet to ask prayers, so the hook's prostration has support in the Rule.
Editor pass: causal 'that's why' softened; obedience described as through the community and its leaders; number removed from a practice example.
